pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: You're laying out a small project as several packages. How do you decide what belongs in each one, and what does a name like `utils` or `common` tell you about a boundary?
expected_points: each package should have a single nameable reason to change (cohesion)
name a package for the job it provides, not the shape of what it contains
utils/common are grab-bags that attract code and make everything depend on them
keep the exported surface small; exported names are commitments

questions.prompt: What is dependency direction, and why must a stable low-level package never import a volatile high-level one?
expected_points: imports should point from volatile (policy, presentation, wiring) toward stable (core types, rules)
an import inherits the imported package's churn: if the core imports presentation, every format change shakes the module everything depends on
the low-level package also becomes impossible to use or test without dragging the high-level one along

questions.prompt: What is an import cycle, why is it a problem even in languages that allow it, and what are two ways to break one?
expected_points: A imports B and B imports A, directly or through a chain
the two units can't be built, understood, or tested separately — one module wearing two names; languages that allow it get init-order bugs
break it by moving the shared piece down into a lower package, passing plain data instead of importing, or inverting with an interface defined by the low side
in Go the compiler rejects cycles outright: 'import cycle not allowed'

questions.prompt: When is one flat package the right choice over several small ones? What does each split cost, and what signals that it's time to split?
expected_points: start flat for small programs or when the seams aren't clear yet
splits cost reader hops, frozen exported surfaces, and early boundary guesses that are breaking changes to undo
split when a cluster has its own reason to change, to hide a decision, or to let the compiler enforce a dependency rule

questions.prompt: Walk me through how you moved the tangled main.go into three packages without breaking behavior. What made that safe?
expected_points: small moves, compiling and running tests after each
bottom-up order: expense (imports nothing) first, then ledger, then report, then main as wiring
green tests plus identical program output are the proof behavior didn't change
move code without changing its logic at the same time

questions.prompt: A low-level storage package needs to notify the UI when data changes, but imports must point down. How does the call get up?
expected_points: the low package defines an interface for what it needs; the high package implements it and injects itself
the call goes up at runtime while the import still points down
io.Writer is this pattern: fmt calls your type without importing your package

questions.prompt: report.Summary takes a map[string]int rather than a *ledger.Ledger. What did that choice buy, and what would the alternative have cost?
expected_points: report needs numbers, not the ledger — passing data removes the report→ledger import edge entirely
report becomes testable with a literal map and reusable for any source of totals
taking the Ledger would couple presentation to storage and add an arrow that must be policed
